source_refs.note: Topic 1.7.2, printed page 8: ionic radius and its trends (Figure 1.5; the printed radii in picometres are not reproduced).

blocks.text: The ionic radius is a measure of the size of an ion in a crystal lattice, defined as the distance from the nucleus of an ion to its outermost electron shell, in picometres or angstroms. When an atom loses one or more electrons to become a positive ion it generally becomes smaller than the neutral atom, because the loss of electrons reduces electronic repulsion and lets the remaining electrons be pulled closer to the nucleus. When an atom gains one or more electrons to become an anion it generally becomes larger than the neutral atom, because the added electrons increase electronic repulsion, the nuclear pull on each electron decreases and the electron cloud expands.

Across a period from left to right the ionic radius of cations decreases, because the increasing nuclear charge pulls the electrons closer; the radius of anions also decreases across a period for the same reason. Down a group both cations and anions increase in size, because the principal quantum number n increases, more electron shells are added, and the greater distance of the outermost electrons from the nucleus outweighs the effect of the increased nuclear charge.

blocks.prompt: Predict and explain the relative sizes of a lithium atom and its ion, an oxygen atom and its oxide ion, and a nitride ion against a fluoride ion.
blocks.explanation: Lithium ion is smaller than the lithium atom: an electron is lost, repulsion falls and the rest are pulled in. The oxide ion is larger than the oxygen atom: two electrons are gained and the cloud expands. Nitride and fluoride have the same number of electrons, but nitrogen has fewer protons, so its nucleus holds the electrons less tightly and the nitride ion is the larger.

items: Ionic radius: nucleus to outermost shell of an ion in a lattice. Cations are smaller than their atoms, anions larger.
Both kinds of ion shrink across a period and grow down a group.
